newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-AMERICAN DOWNHILL DROUGHT LOOKS LIKE CONTINUING.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-AMERICAN DOWNHILL DROUGHT LOOKS LIKE CONTINUING.

text.p: A North American has yet to win the men's downhill world title and as training began on Tuesday there was little to suggest the drought would end in Sestriere.
Over the years the United States and Canada have produced skiers who have dominated the sport's glamour event.
Canada's Crazy Canucks, led by Steve Podborski and Ken Read, and American fliers Billy Johnson and Doug Lewis claimed every major ski racing title, except one -- downhill world champion.
The best the United States can boast is a pair of bronze medals from A.J. Kitt at the 1993 championships and Lewis in 1985.

Despite the exploits of the Crazy Canucks, who won 10 World Cup downhills between 1980 and 1983 and an overall World Cup downhill title by Podborski in 1982, no Canadian has set foot on the podium at the world championships.
Their best results were a pair of fifth places for Brian Stemmle at last year's championships and Rob Boyd in 1987.
Kitt, Boyd and Stemmle are back but are way below top form.
Boyd and Stemmle, who began the season as Canada's top-ranked downhillers, have produced just one top 20 placing between them in eight downhills.
Olympic bronze medallist Ed Podivinskyis the only Canadian downhiller to have cracked the top 10.

"I don't want to say we've given up on the the World Cup season but everyone is pretty bummed out and we're all looking at the worlds and busting one out," said Podivinsky. "One good race could go a long way to salvaging the season."
The American team situation is equally dire.
Training was disrupted earlier in the new year when downhill coach Uli Luthi was jailed for eight days after an altercation with a gendarme in Chamonix, France, during training.
The team then lost top-ranked downhiller Kyle Rasmussen when he sustained torn knee ligaments in a crash in Wengen.

U.S. prospects were lowered even further last weekend in Kitzbuehel when Olympic champion Tommy Moe, who finally appeared to be on his way back from a knee injury that had hindered him for almost two seasons, sliced a tendon in his wrist while serving drinks at a pub popular among the skiers.
U.S. medal hopes will now rest on 28-year-old Kitt's fragile knees and mental state.
Kitt, who injured his knee in Val d'Isere last season, appeared to be over the injury when he finished eighth in Val Gardena just before Christmas.
But he pulled up suddenly in a subsequent race in Chamonix and returned home contemplating retirement.

"I was just burnt out, I needed to recharge my batteries," said Kitt, who finished 51st in the first training run on Tuesday. "It had been a long year rehabilitating my knee. I came out with both barrels blazing and then I just had a huge letdown.
"I don't know what it was, I just couldn't control it. I started to feel it in Bormio. There just wasn't any fire.
"I felt the same way in Chamonix and when I got to Wengen it felt wrong, so I went home. I was worried that maybe I was heading for retirement because I didn't have that spark.
"But after a few days at home I realised all I needed was some rest. Being at home felt wrong."
The injuries will result in the United States fielding only three men in Saturday's race -- Kitt, Chad Fleischer and World Cup rookie Jason Rosener, who was 15th on Tuesday.
